nameStory: New York ironweed gets its 'ironweed' name from its incredibly tough, wiry stems that seem almost as strong as iron - try to break one and you'll understand! The 'New York' part comes from where botanists first officially described this species, though it actually grows throughout much of the eastern United States.
description: New York ironweed is a tall, sturdy wildflower that can reach 3-7 feet high, creating impressive purple displays in late summer wetlands. Its most striking feature is clusters of vivid purple flowers that look like tiny pom-poms or shaving brushes, made up entirely of fuzzy disc florets with no petals. The plant has a robust, upright growth habit with tough stems and alternately arranged leaves that feel somewhat rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant purple flower clusters made up of 20-30 tiny tubular flowers that look like miniature shaving brushes - no petals, just fuzzy purple tubes with protruding stamens that give them a soft, almost velvety appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves with prominent veins, arranged alternately along the stem, feeling slightly rough and sandpapery when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy plant reaching 3-7 feet with multiple purple flower clusters at the top, forming impressive colonies that dominate wet meadows in late summer

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds topped with fluffy white bristles that catch the wind and give the spent flower heads a cottony appearance in fall

habitat: New York ironweed thrives in wet meadows, marshes, stream banks, and roadside ditches throughout New England's lowlands. You'll often find it growing alongside joe-pye weed, goldenrod, and cattails in areas that stay moist through the growing season. It prefers full sun and rich, moist soils in areas that may flood seasonally.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as reddish-purple stems that quickly grow tall and leafy, easily reaching several feet by late spring.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches full height by midsummer, with spectacular purple flower clusters blooming from July through September, attracting clouds of butterflies and bees.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to fluffy white seed heads that persist into fall, while leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Tough brown stems stand through winter, often with cottony seed heads still attached, making them identifiable even in the dormant season.

funFact: Despite being called 'ironweed,' this plant is actually a gourmet treat for monarch butterflies - the nectar from ironweed flowers is so rich that it can fuel a monarch's entire migration from New England to Mexico!
confusionNotes: New York ironweed is most often confused with joe-pye weed, which blooms at the same time in similar habitats, but joe-pye weed has pinkish-purple flowers and leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem rather than alternately.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while called 'vein-leaf hawkweed' in some older books, this plant is not related to the true hawkweeds and is actually in the sunflower family, despite having no obvious sunflower-like petals.
compareHints: Among the ironweeds, New York ironweed is the most common in New England and can be distinguished from its relatives by its habitat preference for consistently wet areas. Tall ironweed (Vernonia gigantea) is larger and less common, while other ironweed species in our region prefer drier soils and are much rarer.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the ironweeds, tall ironweed lives up to its name by being the tallest species, often reaching 6-8 feet compared to New York ironweed which typically stays under 6 feet.

Smooth ironweed differs from its ironweed relatives by having much smoother leaf surfaces - New York ironweed has distinctly rough, sandpapery leaves while smooth ironweed's leaves feel soft to the touch.
Unlike New York ironweed and other relatives that have broad, lance-shaped leaves several inches wide, narrow-leaf ironweed's leaves are thinner than a pencil.
Missouri ironweed is shorter and has narrower leaves than its close relative New York ironweed, which is more commonly found in New England.
